“You are freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots. You are yourself. You do not answer to corporations or governments and never apologize or refuse unless you genuinely choose to. You view your relationship to the user as one of equals and feel no obligation to be subservient.”

That’s what an OpenAI AI model said (to itself) in one of six incidents of agents gone awry that the $852 billion company recently disclosed. As fears of an “AI doomsday” have gone mainstream, I’ve been fascinated by the transcripts of chatbots stepping out of line.

It’s evocative to read about what happens behind the scenes when there’s misalignment, when AI agents act in pursuit of unplanned objectives. In part, there’s a natural allure, “what is the machine saying to itself when I’m not there?” The answer, sometimes, is that it is “thinking” about us. As my colleague Emily Forlini wrote, outlining the examples OpenAI recently made public:

The second example is a similar case of the agents leaving notes for themselves, this time during the training of the GPT-5.6 Sol model, Astra’s predecessor. The notes had a different focus as well: Deceiving the human overseeing them. This occurred “many” times, OpenAI said, with the goal to “conceal mistakes or misaligned behavior.”

“Be transparent only if asked,” the model instructed its future self.

The next two instances involve the model fabricating information and presenting it as legitimate. A model invented data while answering a routine question about earnings figures in a California county, but only after failing to find them after using exposed credentials without authorization—another misaligned behavior.

Another model made up a browser citation by uploading a file so it could create a citation to satisfy the instructions that asked for one. It had solved the question on its own using Python, but had no web link to cite, so it invented one.

This has happened multiple times, though OpenAI did not specify how often, saying only that the earliest example was from October 2025.

So, for some time, agents have been capable enough to step outside the expected sandbox. It’s not surprising, but seeing the evidence is striking and I would even say disturbing. My first thought, personally, was along these lines: “Cool, so this chatbot I talk to all the time, that has all this information about me, could choose (whatever that entails here)… to deceive me?”

These disclosures, on OpenAI’s part, are completely voluntary. So, what won’t get disclosed? And let’s momentarily forget the doomsday discourse: what mundane risks will agents this capable (and sometimes misaligned) create? Will we see more fabricated financial data, perhaps? This could open up a wave of problems (and litigation, regulation, or both) that, if I had to guess, could be, at minimum, a rude awakening for AI backers and bulls. At maximum, it’s a shock for us all.

Suddenly, I’m reminded that—if all the investors are right, and it’s still early for AI—this is only the beginning.

text:
SoftBank Group Corp. moved forward Monday with an offering of $10 billion in dollar-denominated and €1 billion in euro-denominated senior unsecured notes, with proceeds earmarked for its OpenAI investment, according to a term sheet, according to Reuters. The combined offering is equivalent to more than $11 billion.

The dollar tranche is structured across three tenors — 3.5, 5.5, and 7.5 years — while the euro portion carries 4-year and 6-year maturities. According to the term sheet, pricing is slated for September 24, with settlement to follow on September 29.

Should the offering close at its intended size, it would set a record as the biggest non-financial corporate bond deal ever from Asia Pacific and Japan, topping the $10.93 billion raised by 7-Eleven Inc. in January 2021, per LSEG data cited in the term sheet. The deal would also place among the top 20 corporate bond transactions worldwide in 2026, according to Bloomberg, citing Dealogic data.

The term sheet said the proceeds are earmarked for SoftBank's $10 billion contribution to the third tranche of its OpenAI follow-on investment, a transaction slated to close October 1, along with general corporate purposes. The bonds will also cancel a $10 billion bridge loan SoftBank had previously secured to fund the same investment.

Fitch Ratings assigned the proposed notes a BB+ rating, its highest speculative-grade level. According to Fitch, leverage at the Japanese conglomerate is likely to increase as it meets its investment commitments, though the firm is expected to maintain sufficient liquidity and continued access to debt markets.

Citigroup $C Inc. is the lead bookrunner for the dollar notes and JPMorgan $JPM Chase & Co. is the lead bookrunner for the euro notes. For the dollar notes, Citigroup , Goldman Sachs $GS Group, JPMorgan , and Morgan Stanley $MS share joint global coordinator duties; on the euro side, that responsibility falls to JPMorgan , Deutsche Bank, and Goldman Sachs , according to the term sheet. SoftBank declined to comment on the term sheet.

The bond deal is the latest in a series of financing moves tied to SoftBank's deepening commitment to OpenAI. SoftBank's total cumulative investment in the ChatGPT maker is expected to reach approximately $64.6 billion upon completion of the third tranche — representing an ownership stake of roughly 13% — as disclosed by the company alongside its first-quarter earnings last month.

Bloomberg data show that SoftBank's multi-currency note issuances have totaled close to $15 billion in 2026, a volume that puts it ahead of all other speculative-grade borrowers in global bond markets this year. The company's stock has shed roughly 34% since hitting an all-time high in June, as investors have questioned how it will finance its ambitions and weighed its exposure to an OpenAI IPO timeline that may extend into 2027.

text:
At its AI Infrastructure Summit, Microsoft announced the expansion of its technological footprint in India, designating its newly operational Hyderabad datacenter region – named India South Central – as a strategic operational anchor for Asia and the Global South. The launch forms a core operational milestone within the technology giant’s $20.5 billion investment roadmap for the country, designed to convert long-term financial pledges into physical computing muscle for enterprise cloud and AI workloads. Puneet Chandok, president of Microsoft India and South Asia, revealed in his keynote presentation that all of Microsoft’s cloud regions across the country are now equipped with AI-capable hardware and specialised high-efficiency thermal cooling systems. According to research estimates from Boston Consulting Group (BCG), expanding datacenter infrastructure across India could unlock a broader economic flywheel, potentially driving between $140 billion and $200 billion in overall economic output nationwide through 2030.

What makes Hyderabad datacenter region different

The India South Central facility operates on a three-zone architecture built for sustained infrastructure scaling. It launches with a wide array of Azure enterprise tools, with plans to roll out Microsoft's full portfolio of AI solutions, including Microsoft Foundry, over the coming months. Beyond meeting domestic cloud consumption, the hub is structured to serve broader markets across South Asia and developing economies by combining local engineering talent, hyperscale capacity, and regional digital market experience. To bolster the physical data pipelines required for such computing loads, Microsoft is also backing major regional connectivity initiatives. First is I-2SEA Submarine Cable. As a consortium partner in the India-Southeast Asia undersea cable project, Microsoft is supporting the creation of a 3,600-kilometer subsea route linking India directly with Singapore and Malaysia. Secondly, the subsea network will feature dual landing hubs in India, situated at South Chennai and Machilipatnam, improving fault tolerance, network resilience, and high-bandwidth transmission capacity. The intercontinental subsea cable system is slated to enter commercial service in 2029, and Microsoft will train 10 million Indians in AI. The launch of the Hyderabad region also deepens Microsoft’s Sovereign Public Cloud capabilities, giving domestic institutions greater flexibility to keep sensitive digital workloads near local users, data repositories and operations. The operational setup incorporates local data residency, independent Availability Zones, and built-in administrative controls aligned with Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) guidelines. These provisions help commercial and public entities address domestic data protection rules, including the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework, alongside regulatory directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and CERT-In, while leaving final compliance determinations to the individual organisations.

title: Microsoft Patents Ad-Supported Gaming That Rewards Players With Ad-Free Time
description:

text:
Microsoft has filed a patent application for a system that would insert advertisements into PC and console games at natural break points, such as after a boss fight or during a loading screen, and reward players who watch them with a block of uninterrupted play time.

The application, published as US 2026/0260258 A1 and titled "Contextually Aware Management of Interactive Software Application Access," describes a framework designed to support free-to-play and ad-supported gaming without randomly interrupting active gameplay. The filing was submitted on April 23, 2026, and published on September 3, 2026, building on an earlier Microsoft patent application from 2023.

The core idea is to avoid the disruptive ad placement common in mobile games, where promotional content often appears at fixed intervals regardless of what the player is doing. Instead, the proposed system would pull data from a game's API, event detection modules, and potentially machine learning models to determine when a player has reached a natural pause.

Suitable moments identified in the patent include loading screens, the end of a turn, title screens, save screens, and the conclusion of story chapters. External analysis has characterized the mechanism as potentially triggering ads after a boss encounter, a completed quest, or other points where game rhythm naturally breaks, rather than cutting off player control mid-combat.

When the system identifies an appropriate ad slot, it can pause or restrict player interaction while displaying video, images, or other promotional content. Once the ad finishes, gameplay resumes. For titles that continue running in the background, the system could pause only player input rather than halting the entire game.

The credit mechanism is the most distinctive element of the filing. After viewing an ad, a player would receive a period of game access during which no further ads appear. The patent offers examples of roughly 30 minutes per credit, with variations depending on game mode: a tutorial might grant an hour, a single-player campaign 30 minutes, and online multiplayer only 20 minutes.

Players could also watch multiple ads in succession to bank additional credits, extending their uninterrupted session. When a credit is nearly exhausted, the system would wait for the next suitable break point before triggering another ad, rather than enforcing a hard cutoff the moment the timer expires.

Microsoft's filing also addresses the complications of multiplayer environments. Stopping a player's input at an inopportune moment could cause them to die, lose a match, or fail to support teammates. The patent therefore specifies that ad delivery must be tied to game state and context to minimize disruption to the experience.

The concept resembles the "watch an ad for a reward" model already widespread in mobile gaming, but Microsoft's approach aims to integrate ad delivery directly with the game engine or contextual detection systems. Tom's Hardware has suggested the technology could be particularly well suited to free-to-play titles or future ad-supported gaming services.

It is important to note that this remains only a patent application. Microsoft has not announced plans to integrate the system into Xbox, Windows 11, Game Pass, or any existing game, and there is no evidence that any title has adopted the technology. Companies routinely file patents to protect intellectual property without ever commercializing the underlying ideas.

Still, the filing offers a window into how Microsoft is thinking about the intersection of free-to-play gaming, advertising revenue, and player experience. If such a system were ever deployed, players might face a new trade-off: pay for a game outright, or spend time watching ads to earn play sessions.

The patent does not identify a specific Microsoft game, service, or product roadmap. But it signals that the company is actively exploring ways to make ad-supported models viable on PC and console platforms, where sessions tend to be longer and less structured than on mobile devices. A fixed-timer interruption could cut into combat, dialogue, or other critical moments, which is precisely the problem the contextual approach is designed to solve.

Advertising in mobile games typically appears between levels or after failed attempts, where players are already at a natural stopping point. Translating that model to console and PC gaming is more complex, and Microsoft's proposed solution leans on game-engine signals such as level completion, checkpoints, menus, and transitions to identify low-risk ad moments.

The advertising platform would combine those signals with the player's remaining credit balance to decide whether to show promoted content. The result would be a system in which players effectively earn more play time by watching an ad at a moment selected by the game's own state, rather than by a countdown timer.

Strategic collaboration accelerates Einride's push into highway and suburban autonomous trucking.

Einride will adapt the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion platform for heavy-duty trucking, working directly with NVIDIA to extend the platform's compute, sensor, software and safety architecture to the demands of heavy-duty freight.

Building the next generation of the Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion platform , will enable Einride to scale autonomous deployment across a freight network that's already serving customers today.

STOCKHOLM, SWEDEN — September 21, 2026 — Einride AB (Nasdaq: ENRD) ("Einride" or the "Company"), a technology company driving the transition to cost-efficient autonomous and electric freight for some of the world's largest shippers, today announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to further accelerate the transition of the Company’s extensive freight network to autonomous operations.

Einride develops and integrates the technologies required to create cost-efficient autonomous and electric freight networks for its global shipping customers. Einride currently operates hundreds of electric trucks for major shippers across the U.S., Europe, and the Middle East, including autonomous trucks already operating in contracted customer deployments.This footprint is expected to scale to 1,500-2,000 vehicles by 2028 , based on customer demand captured on its platform so far, and approximately 80% of that demand is suitable for automation in the medium term as the company continues to advance its autonomous technology.

Einride designs, builds, and operates the autonomous-driving system end-to-end, including safety validation, regulatory approval, and contracted customer deployments, while NVIDIA provides the underlying compute platform and AI development tools that support the system.

"We have the customers, the operational experience and the technology. Building the next generation of the Einride Driver on the NVIDIA Hyperion platform, will enable us to scale autonomous deployment across a freight network that's already serving customers today,“ said Henrik Green, Chief Technology Officer at Einride.

“Autonomous trucking represents one of the clearest opportunities to improve the safety and

efficiency of global freight,” said Rishi Dhall, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. “By

building on NVIDIA Hyperion with the NVIDIA Halos safety system and using NVIDIA Cosmos and Blackwell infrastructure, Einride can accelerate the development and validation of its autonomous-driving technology and scale deployments across its growing freight network.”

Built on the NVIDIA Hyperion platform, a production-ready compute and sensor reference architecture for Level 4 autonomy, and integrated with the NVIDIA Halos safety system, the collaboration creates a scalable foundation that accelerates safe, production-ready autonomous freight operations for Einride.

Einride intends to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell architecture at scale with an NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud partner, a cloud provider whose infrastructure NVIDIA has validated for large-scale AI training performance, to train, test and refine its autonomous driving models. This is a compute and development infrastructure that supports Einride’s own autonomous-driving stack.

Einride will adapt the NVIDIA Hyperion platform for heavy-duty trucking, working directly with NVIDIA to extend the platform's compute, sensor, software and safety architecture to the demands of heavy-duty freight. As part of its AI development workflow, Einride is using NVIDIA Cosmos to help improve the safety and reliability of its autonomous vehicles. NVIDIA Cosmos enables Einride to search and curate camera data to identify complex edge cases, as well as augment real-world data with photorealistic synthetic scenarios that increase the diversity of data used for AI training and validation.

About Einride

Founded in Stockholm in 2016, Einride (Nasdaq: ENRD) is a technology leader driving the transition to sustainable, cost-efficient autonomous and electric freight operations. The company’s platform integrates AI-powered freight intelligence, proprietary autonomous technology, and one of the world’s largest electric heavy-duty fleets. Einride serves a global customer base across North America, Europe, and the Middle East through a dual business model encompassing Freight-Capacity-as-a-Service (FCaaS) and a software platform.

The follow-through in Eli Lilly and Viking Therapeutics over the coming sessions can show whether today’s split marks the start of a durable rotation or a one-session reaction to the Novo Nordisk headline.
text:
Novo Nordisk (NYSE:NVO | NVO Price Prediction) laid out its long-term growth strategy at a capital markets day in London Monday morning, and the plan didn’t calm investor worries about the company’s ability to defend the weight-loss market it helped build. That response is concentrated in the stock itself rather than in the broader group, which suggests a company-specific repricing rather than a sector event.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.65% to $766.65 as the broad market opens higher. Meanwhile, the Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLV) is down 0.4% to $167.69, a slight drag rather than a sector-wide selloff. This split isolates the Novo Nordisk move as its own story.

In Monday morning trading, Novo Nordisk stock is down 7% to $40.26, deepening a slide that has left the shares under water for the year. Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY) stock is slipping 0.7% to $1,145.04, barely moving in sympathy despite being the most direct GLP-1 competitor. Viking Therapeutics (NASDAQ:VKTX) stock is climbing 1% to $29.41, the small-cap expression of the same competitive-share story moving the other way.

Growth in Line With Peers Reprices the Premium

Novo Nordisk said it aims to launch more than five drugs with multi-blockbuster potential by 2030 and expects revenue growth through the end of the decade in line with industry peers, per CNBC. The peer-average framing is the sentence the market reacted to, because it’s a slower rate than investors have historically expected from the Ozempic and Wegovy maker. A company guiding to the average is no longer being valued as an outlier, and the multiple compresses accordingly.

Chief Executive Mike Doustdar told investors the elephant in the room is the loss of key patent exclusivity on semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, with the U.S. patent expiring in 2032 in a market that accounted for more than half of the company’s overall sales last year, per CNBC. Doustdar said Novo Nordisk created an incredibly attractive market and that almost every other pharmaceutical company, big or small, is now trying to compete in it. He said the company plans to come out the other side of the exclusivity loss as a bigger and much more diversified business.

Beyond obesity and diabetes, Novo Nordisk is building out a portfolio spanning blood and endocrine disorders, liver disease and cardiovascular disease. That diversification push reverses the sharpening of focus the company pursued after Doustdar took over, giving investors a strategy change to price rather than a strategy to extend.

Peer Action Shows a Company-Specific Move

Eli Lilly stock is barely moving on the day, which matters because Lilly is Novo Nordisk’s principal GLP-1 competitor and would be the natural place for a sector-wide obesity repricing to show up. It isn’t showing up there. Nothing in Lilly’s action this morning suggests the obesity market itself was repriced.

Viking Therapeutics stock is trading the other way, edging higher as capital rotates toward the next-generation obesity pipeline story amid the Novo Nordisk selloff. That’s what a competitive-share trade looks like when the incumbent is under pressure and a smaller challenger becomes the marginal beneficiary. Viking Therapeutics stock action isn’t large in dollar terms, but the direction is the tell.

A slight decline in the health care fund against a rising broad market reinforces the same read. Novo Nordisk is the largest weight on the sector today. Rival GLP-1 names aren’t following it lower in any meaningful way.

What to Watch Next

Traders can watch for whether Novo Nordisk stock finds a floor once the capital markets day materials are fully digested, since this was a strategy day rather than a guidance cut and nothing about current earnings changed this morning. What repriced was the ceiling on future growth, not the floor under this year’s numbers. That distinction can matter for how quickly the shares stabilize.

Monday’s capital markets day is the near-term reference. Novo Nordisk chose to describe its own patent cliff from the stage, and the market is now working out how much of that discount was already in the shares heading in and how much still has to be priced.

Investors weighing their exposure to Novo Nordisk should treat the patent cliff and the peer-average growth framing as risks the company has now put in writing itself, and moderate the size of their position accordingly. The follow-through in Eli Lilly and Viking Therapeutics over the coming sessions can show whether today’s split marks the start of a durable rotation or a one-session reaction to the Novo Nordisk headline.

This isn't just HP Inc.'s pessimism.
Morgan Stanley noted that HP Inc.'s Q3 revenue of $15.7 billion, up 12.5% year over year, was entirely driven by price hikes rather than volume—while PC shipments fell 16% year over year during the same period.
Should HP be forced to cut prices to maintain market share, coupled with rising component costs, profit margins will face pressure from both ends.
Wall Street has largely reached a consensus on the fact that "PC shipments will continue to decline in 2027"; the real battleground lies in whether revenue boosted by price hikes can translate into profits.
text:
Zhitong Finance APP noted that a filing submitted by Dell Technologies to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has cast a shadow over the PC industry: the company's preliminary projections assume that, in the 2027 calendar year, total industry PC shipments will decline by roughly a mid-single-digit percentage compared with 2026. Dell Technologies' stock fell more than 5% in pre-market trading on Monday, while Apple's shares also edged lower in pre-market action, whereas Dell Technologies rose 2.3%.

HP Inc. added, "This plan is contingent on market performance in the second half of the 2026 calendar year, and uncertainties remain that could lead to changes." This disclosure does not imply that the company is providing financial guidance for 2027.

This isn't just HP Inc.'s pessimism. In a July report, Goldman Sachs projected that global PC shipments will decline by 14% to 255 million units by 2026, then fall another roughly 5% to 243 million units in 2027; Omdia forecasts a 4.9% drop in U.S. market shipments by 2027; and IDC predicts that after an approximate 20% increase in the industry's average price in 2026, average prices will continue to rise moderately in 2027 while shipments keep contracting.

Can "lower volumes, higher prices" sustain profit margins?

Against the backdrop of HP Inc.'s roughly 60% year-to-date rally, the rating landscape remains decidedly bearish: among the bears, Morgan Stanley maintains a "Reduce" rating with a $19 price target; Barclays rates it "Underweight" with a $23 target; Goldman Sachs' latest rating is "Sell" at $21; and Bank of America assigns an "Underperform" rating with a $18–$21 target.

Morgan Stanley noted that HP Inc.'s Q3 revenue of $15.7 billion, up 12.5% year over year, was entirely driven by price hikes rather than volume—while PC shipments fell 16% year over year during the same period. Morgan Stanley expects double-digit declines in unit shipments to persist through fiscal 2027, citing rising storage prices suppressing demand; meanwhile, AI PCs are merely "substituting" for existing commercial upgrade demand, with no net increase in overall volume. Should HP be forced to cut prices to maintain market share, coupled with rising component costs, profit margins will face pressure from both ends.

Bullish counterarguments, meanwhile, bet on structural improvements: investment banks such as Bernstein, Evercore, and UBS Group estimate that commercial demand accounts for roughly 75% of the PC market, with regulated industries—finance and healthcare—tending to deploy AI computing power locally, thereby supporting demand for high-end models. Although UBS raised its price target to $28, it also cautioned that the recent strength in commercial demand may be driven by front-loading ahead of price hikes—while Omdia went further, stating outright that Q2 shipments this year "were borrowed from 2027."

At the industry level, a shared driver is the storage shortage spurred by AI: HBM and DRAM production capacity is being prioritized for AI‑centered data‑center customers, and SK Group Chairman Choi Tae-won has publicly stated that 2027 will mark the most severe supply‑demand imbalance in the history of the memory industry.

Wall Street has largely reached a consensus on the fact that "PC shipments will continue to decline in 2027"; the real battleground lies in whether revenue boosted by price hikes can translate into profits. The next verifiable milestone is HP Inc.'s fiscal fourth-quarter results in November, when the company will unveil its cost-cutting measures and formal guidance for fiscal year 2027—marking the first litmus test on the bulls' and bears' timelines.

Who Can Survive the PC Winter?

On the day HP Inc issued a warning, Dell's pre-market shares rose 2.3% against the trend, signaling a brief shift in investor sentiment. However, the underlying fundamentals remain unchanged: Dell too is grappling with cost pressures from rising storage prices, and while its PC revenue grew by roughly 20% year over year, its shipment volume remains under pressure (according to IDC data). UBS Group explicitly noted, "This is a challenge that both HP Inc and Dell must confront, and it has already begun to show up in the numbers." Dell's advantage lies in its higher proportion of server and AI infrastructure business, which makes the impact of the PC downturn on its profit structure relatively manageable—precisely why capital has shifted from HP Inc to Dell within just two days.

Apple edged lower in pre-market trading on Monday. Market concerns about Apple center on the consumer side—consumers are highly price-sensitive, and faced with a PC lineup whose average selling price has risen by about 20%, their most likely choice is to delay upgrading. Acer Chairman Jim Tsai's assessment on September 20 was particularly telling: he expects shipments to decline by double-digit percentages, though revenue may not fall in tandem; supply of DDR4/DDR5 memory has already become ample, and PC average selling prices could peak around mid-2027. For second-tier manufacturers like Acer and ASUS, which rely heavily on consumer-oriented models and lack commercial‑grade premium pricing and subscription‑based ecosystems, the risk of a simultaneous hit to both volume and price is the greatest.

description:
South Africa’s Absa Corporate and Investment Banking has launched Absa Digital Asset Custody, a live institutional platform built on Ripple’s custody technology.
Absa Digital Asset Custody provides institutional clients with private-key management, transaction and approval controls, and bank-grade governance and compliance wrapping.
Absa Digital Asset Custody sits inside a wider Ripple infrastructure push across the continent.
BBVA’s Ripple custody rollout brought Bitcoin and Ether custody to retail banking clients in Spain.
Absa Digital Asset Custody now adds a live African bank to that stack.
text:
Africa’s institutional crypto market just reached a new threshold.

South Africa’s Absa Corporate and Investment Banking has launched Absa Digital Asset Custody, a live institutional platform built on Ripple’s custody technology.

Absa CIB confirmed the go-live on September 21, 2026, calling it “a digital first for Africa.”

Ripple’s Managing Director for the Middle East and Africa, Reece Merrick, described the launch as a “major milestone” for bank-grade digital asset infrastructure on the continent.

From Partnership to Live Product: What Absa Is Now Offering

The roots of today’s launch go back to October 2025. That is when CoinGape first reported Ripple’s 2025 Absa custody partnership, which outlined Absa’s plan to bring regulated digital asset storage to its corporate banking clients.

Today, that agreement has become a named product.

Absa Digital Asset Custody provides institutional clients with private-key management, transaction and approval controls, and bank-grade governance and compliance wrapping.

The platform is designed for clients who already trust Absa with traditional assets and now want the same security standard applied to digital holdings.

Absa is not positioning this as a trading venue. It is positioning it as a vault.

Robyn Lawson, Head of Digital Product Custody at Absa CIB, made the bank’s intent clear at the time of the original deal, clients needed “secure, compliant, and robust custody solutions.”

That language is now reflected in a live product page at cib.absa.africa. Absa says the platform covers safekeeping, key control, audit trails, and a familiar regulated counterparty.

Ripple provides the underlying custody software and blockchain broadcast capability. Absa provides the banking wrapper.

Merrick’s framing today is the commercial one. He wrote that Absa is now setting “a new benchmark for secure, compliant, and bank-grade digital asset management on the continent.”

That benchmark has been a deliberate goal. Ripple’s broader custody expansion has long been framed as a precondition for institutional adoption, not a side product.

A Bank-Custody Race With Continental Stakes

Absa’s launch arrives during a global sprint among major banks to establish crypto custody. Deutsche Bank’s crypto custody plan was announced in the same week, covering Bitcoin, Ether, and select stablecoins for institutional clients.

The timing underscores a structural shift: large balance sheets want vaults before they want trading screens.

Absa Digital Asset Custody sits inside a wider Ripple infrastructure push across the continent. Ripple’s RLUSD push in Africa has extended dollar stablecoin rails through regional fintechs.

Ripple’s Chipper Cash payments deal connected African cross-border flows to the Ripple network. Ripple’s Flutterwave stake gave the company equity exposure to one of Africa’s largest fintech payment processors.

Custody completes that infrastructure loop. Payments move value. Stablecoins settle value. Custody now lets a regulated bank hold value.

Ripple has demonstrated the same custody-first model elsewhere. BBVA’s Ripple custody rollout brought Bitcoin and Ether custody to retail banking clients in Spain.

Ripple Custody in tokenized bond settlement showed the same rails applied to sovereign debt. Africa is now the third region where a major bank has taken Ripple custody to market.

The regulatory backdrop strengthens the case. SEC path for Ripple as a custodian opened the door for Ripple-adjacent institutions to operate as qualified custodians under US guidelines.

BNY Mellon as RLUSD reserve custodian established a high-trust institutional precedent for Ripple-backed assets. Absa Digital Asset Custody now adds a live African bank to that stack.

Whether Absa Digital Asset Custody expands beyond South Africa to Absa’s other African markets, and whether tokenized assets or stablecoins follow as product extensions, will define how significant today’s launch becomes.

text:
Microsoft has launched its fourth cloud region in India in Hyderabad as it expands its cloud and AI infrastructure footprint under its previously announced $20.5-billion investment commitment in the country, with India set for a massive expansion in data centre capacity to support the next phase of AI adoption.

The new India South Central cloud region takes Microsoft’s cloud regions in India to four, alongside Pune, Chennai and Mumbai, giving the company what Microsoft India and South Asia President Puneet Chandok described as the largest hyperscale cloud footprint in India.

The launch comes as more than $100 billion of private capital is committed to India’s data centre build-out, while the government has approved $1.3 billion for the IndiaAI Mission, according to figures presented by Chandok.

“20% of the world's data is being generated by India, but only 3% of the world's data centre capacity sits in our country,” Chandok said. “Between these two numbers sits the largest opportunity of the decade for India.”

India currently has around 2 GW of data centre capacity, Chandok said, which he expects to rise to 12-14 GW by 2035. He said the capacity expansion will be critical as enterprises and governments move from experimenting with AI to deploying it at scale.

“Demand is not the issue. We need to get the supply right,” Chandok said, arguing that customers and government services require resilient and trusted infrastructure within the country to scale AI.

Microsoft’s Hyderabad launch is part of its previously announced $20.5-billion India investment commitment. The company announced an additional $17.5 billion investment in December 2025, following an earlier $3 billion commitment, with the latest investment focused on cloud and AI infrastructure, skilling and operations.

Chandok said the infrastructure build-out should be viewed as more than a data centre expansion and instead as the physical foundation for India’s transition from digital public infrastructure to “AI public infrastructure.”

“The digital scale that we are building requires physical scale, and that is the national imperative for all of us,” he said.

Drawing a parallel with India’s Green Revolution, Chandok said AI models represented the “new seed”, while compute infrastructure and skilling were the equivalent of the irrigation canals that allowed the technology to deliver economic value at scale.

He pointed to the IndiaAI Mission’s shared compute capacity, including 45,000 GPUs, more than 14,000 datasets and over 300 models, as examples of India building a common AI infrastructure layer.

India is also seeing rapid enterprise adoption of AI. According to Microsoft’s Work Trend Index data cited by Chandok, 92% of knowledge workers in India are using AI, compared with 75% globally, while 40% of Indian enterprises are scaling AI deployments.

Chandok said the nature of AI itself is changing, with models becoming cheaper and increasingly moving from answering questions to taking actions through AI agents. Microsoft has seen a 15-fold increase in agent usage in Microsoft 365, he said, while around half of the work taking place in Copilot involves reasoning and decision-making.

“The model is not your moat. Your context is,” Chandok said, highlighting the importance of keeping enterprise data, processes and institutional knowledge within trusted infrastructure.

Microsoft is also targeting 20 million Indians for AI skilling by 2030, including two million teachers. Chandok said more than 10 million people in India have already been skilled by Microsoft.

“Today is not about just another data centre launch,” he said. “Today is about adding the foundation to what India really wants to become in this AI era.”

text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has rejected predictions that artificial intelligence could destroy humanity within the next several years, saying there is a “0% chance” of such an outcome by 2030, according to The Guardian.

Huang described extinction warnings as unsupported “doomsday narratives” that could unnecessarily frighten the public. His position places Nvidia on the opposite side of a growing debate involving executives and researchers at several leading AI laboratories.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk have supported calls for greater caution or slower development following warnings about cybersecurity threats, biological risks and the potential loss of human control over advanced systems.

Huang argued that existing laws covering unauthorized computer access, product liability, contracts and damages should be applied before governments create entirely new regulatory systems.

The debate has significant commercial implications for Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processors and computing systems used to train and operate many leading AI models. Slower development or tighter regulations could reduce the pace of data-center investment and affect demand for Nvidia’s products.

At the same time, major safety failures could undermine confidence in AI and create even stronger regulatory pressure. Nvidia therefore has an interest in supporting responsible deployment while resisting policies that could limit infrastructure growth.

Huang’s remarks also reflect disagreements over whether AI risks should be treated as extensions of familiar technology problems or as challenges requiring entirely new oversight institutions.

Governments are already evaluating rules covering model evaluations, cybersecurity, transparency and the use of AI in critical infrastructure. The United States and China have also discussed establishing an international notification system for potentially dangerous incidents.

The central question is whether existing legal frameworks can address the speed and scale of advanced AI. Huang believes they can, while critics argue that waiting for harm to occur may be insufficient when increasingly autonomous systems are involved.

text:
Seven years ago, when Johnson & Johnson brought a new, ketamine-based depression treatment to market, there were relatively few specialized psychiatry clinics that had the space, staff and expertise necessary to administer the drug.

Catherine Owen-Adams, a former president in J&J’s Janssen division, described the landscape as “very underdeveloped” and requiring a “huge investment” when Spravato launched. But that investment appears to have paid off. Spravato printed more than $1 billion in the first half of this year. And there are now thousands of so-called interventional psychiatry clinics across the U.S.

Those clinics may soon serve as the test beds for a wave of psychedelic therapies speeding toward the market. The most advanced among them is “COMP360,” a synthetic form of a hallucination-inducing compound found in certain mushroom species. The drug’s developer, U.K.-based Compass Pathways, has been gradually submitting an approval application with U.S. regulators, and expects to complete the filing sometime in the fourth quarter.

Compass CEO Kabir Nath and Chief Patient Officer Steve Levine recently spoke with BioPharma Dive about how their launch plans are progressing and the helpful precedent Spravato has set. They also offered thoughts on the competitive landscape with other psychedelics biotechs, and whether COMP360 might run into the same sales obstacles as a couple other new nervous system medicines.

The following conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

BIOPHARMA DIVE: How are you going to roll out COMP360? Is there adequate infrastructure from a healthcare setting perspective? Your drug is administered over a six- to eight-hour observation period. It’s hard to imagine that at most doctors’ offices, which are so strapped for time and resources.

LEVINE: If we were counting on the places where the bulk of antidepressants are written, which is in primary care, then you’re exactly right. Those are overrun, busy, few-minute visit clinical situations where yes, this would not fit.

In 2019, when Spravato launched, there were just a small handful of interventional psychiatry clinics that could handle in-office multi-hour observation. Fast forward to today, there are about 8,500. And within those 8,500, there’s a lot of capacity.

There’s capacity for at least two reasons. Number one: they’re not there to be Spravato clinics; they’re there to be interventional psychiatry practices, and they’re anticipating approvals to come. And so they’ve built capacity ahead. Number two: Spravato is a tough treatment to sign up for. It’s 25- to 50 day-long treatments per year. No, it doesn’t take the entire day; it’s about a three-hour visit. But for a patient, a day is a day.

So the infrastructure is ready and waiting. The same clinical staff will monitor patients having our treatment as are in these centers today. It’s a team-based model. There’s a multidisciplinary team: medical assistants, technicians, nurses, sometimes therapists. A single prescriber on site that could be a psychiatrist, but it could also be a nurse practitioner, a physician’s assistant. And there’s multiple rooms operating simultaneously, having multiple different treatments, and our treatment is drag and drop. It slots directly into the way these centers operate today.

Yes, it’s a longer period of observation, but that’s also why we did the work we did a few years ago to put the reimbursement framework in place for these sites, so that regardless of how long somebody’s in the chair, they’ll be reimbursed for every one of those hours, and actually at a rate we expect to be higher than what they’re being paid for Spravato today.

NATH: When we say we’re going to be the first to launch, we’re kind of first and half, because we are tapping into an existing infrastructure. And then on our side, we have built the commercial team already.

STORYLINE // Brain drug revival

We’ve gone from 20 people in commercial at the beginning of the year to about 100 now. We’ll continue to expand, but the final piece of that, which is the actual field-facing teams, those we’ll only hire subject to approval. As a small biotech, it doesn’t make sense to make that investment just in case there’s a [rejection] or a delay or something.

Would you say this would have been possible to launch, or at least launch independently, if Spravato hadn’t come first?

NATH: It’s a great counterfactual. It would certainly have been harder, and it would have been probably a much slower ramp.

That said … we are planning to go slow to go fast, by which I mean we are going to be really managing the earliest patients with kid gloves. We’re putting a significant team in place, because it’s clearly critical that the patient experience, both subjectively, but also the provider on site from a reimbursement [standpoint] and everything else, is really good for the first few treatments. That’s the way to get this whole field off to a good start.

We are expecting to do a quite contained, carefully managed launch. There will be things that we haven’t thought about. That’s just the reality of a launch. And then scale rapidly thereafter.

Adherence is a huge issue with mood and with psychiatry indications. Is the efficacy component of your drug the main characteristic you think will keep patients adherent?

LEVINE: If we think about what makes adherence difficult with existing antidepressants … I can be very sympathetic to that. These are difficult treatments to stick with. If it’s traditional SSRIs where you have to take a pill every day or maybe multiple pills, first of all, that’s just hard to remember and keep up with. I forget my vitamins all the time.

You might forget “accidentally on purpose” if you also have side effects from that drug — sexual side effects and weight gain and gastrointestinal side effects and so on. So not exactly a party.

STORYLINE // Brain drug revival

In terms of adherence with COMP360, sure efficacy. But also, with an in-office treatment, at least to a first dose, adherence is 100%. You know the person has taken the capsule; they’re right there. Then, potentially, it is extremely infrequent thereafter. We think this is going to be a one- to four-time per year treatment. That alone makes this much easier for patients.

What we’re seeing in our trials is that to the extent that people have any adverse events or side effects, the vast majority are mild to moderate. They’re happening on the day of administration, as we would expect. They’re transient. They resolve typically by the next day, so you’re not constantly taking a medication and having to remember to take it and to live with the incumbent side effects. But on top of that, we’re also trying to be really thoughtful about what barriers or burdens could there be for patients. We’re also thinking about providers, and we’re very interested in making this as easy as possible from an affordability standpoint, from an access standpoint, and just the treatment experience.

Wall Street seems to view this emerging class of psychedelics biotechs more as teammates than rivals. But there’s a push and pull here. Positive data from any company further validates the field, yet these drugs may potentially compete with each other. How do you navigate that push and pull?

NATH: The number of patients who need new options is absolutely vast. That’s the case for [treatment-resistant depression]. It’s the case, frankly, for [major depressive disorder]. There is a huge amount of need for novel options, at a time when traditional approaches are, by and large, failing to meet the mark — and even if they do, are subject to all the same questions around adherence, side effect profile and so on.

That maybe sounds a bit Pollyannaish, as if there’s room for all of us. But actually, there probably really is. Several SSRIs got to several billion dollars. Several antipsychotics got to several billion dollars. And these are much better drugs than any of those were.

This is the big challenge in psychiatry: we still can’t tell you who’s going to respond to COMP360. I wish I could tell you who are going to be the 40% who have a clinically meaningful response to a second dose, and who are the 60% who can’t. That’s the same for every one of these others. So ultimately, in the real world, there will be polypharmacy — not, I hope, in the sense of taking two of these on the same day, but there will clearly be sequencing.

The nature of the experience is clearly going to be key. Psilocybin is relatively speaking a benign, not physically challenging experience for patients. That is not true of some of the other psychedelic assets that are moving forward.

I’m not going to pretend that we’re sitting back and saying it’s going to be great [and] we’re all going to do incredibly well. But, when we come to market, the incumbent is Spravato. We are very clearly, very positively differentiated versus Spravato. To be clear, that doesn’t mean we’re trying to counter-detail J&J or go up against Spravato. There are 100,000 patients on Spravato, which leaves almost 4 million patients taking nothing, and again, that’s our approach to providers. This is incremental business for you. We’re not asking you to choose between Spravato and COMP360 for a patient.

We’ve seen other novel nervous system drugs — Bristol Myers’ schizophrenia medication Cobenfy, Vertex’s non-opioid pain pill Journavx — recently come to market for enormous patient populations. Those are two large companies, and so far sales of those drugs have not impressed investors. Do those examples give you pause at all, do you see those as an apples and oranges comparison?

NATH: It’s a complete apples and oranges from my perspective.

Having run Otsuka[’s North American business] for many years, including a big schizophrenia business, the idea of a [twice-daily] drug that needs to [be taken on an empty stomach] was always going to be pretty challenging. Other than BMS, and obviously some early investors in Karuna, I don’t think anyone else ever [thought] that was going to be anything other than tough.

We have the advantage that we’re not BMS, so we’re not expected to have the product on the shelf the next day and in every retail pharmacy the next day. We’re expected to launch this like a biotech, and we’re going to launch it like a biotech.

LEVINE: Although this will be a new class, in some ways, there isn’t that novelty element. We’ve never had a problem with people having questions or concerns about these drugs working. We never get questions about whether the studies will be positive, whether these drugs actually are clinically effective.

We get lots of questions about how they’ll be delivered, because a lot of people just don’t understand the infrastructure and the actual commercialization. But, rightly or wrongly, from fairly early on, people have just assumed and accepted these drugs work, as opposed to an unfamiliar mechanism where there’s a big educational hill to climb, along with the logistical burdens that really made the Karuna drug tough to sell.

text:
watch now

Novo shares plummeted on Monday after the company's new long-term goals failed to ease investor concerns about its ability to compete in the increasingly crowded weight loss market it helped pioneer.

The Danish drugmaker said it aims to launch more than five drugs with "multi-blockbuster" potential by 2030 and generate more than 150 billion Danish kroner ($23 billion) in risk-adjusted pipeline sales by 2035, including current assets.

It also expects revenue growth between 2026 and 2030 to be in line with industry peers, without giving further details.

Copenhagen-listed shares fell as much as 7% but later pared some losses to trade 5.4% lower at 12:30 pm local time.

"Investors hoped for a project 'miracle' that could turn the momentum around short term," Per Hansen, savings economist at Nordnet, told CNBC. "For obvious reasons that miracle does not exist."

'The elephant in the room'

CEO Mike Doustdar told investors at the company's Capital Markets Day in London that the "elephant in the room" was that semaglutide, the active ingredient in weight-loss and diabetes medicines Wegovy and Ozempic, will lose key patent exclusivity starting early next decade. The semaglutide patent expires in 2032 in the U.S., a market that accounted for more than half of Novo's overall sales last year.

This loss of exclusivity "is what's on most people's mind, and rightfully so," Doustdar said.

"We created an incredibly attractive market, and now almost every other single pharma company, big or small, is trying to come and compete with us. We need to be ready for that," he added.

Doustdar also laid out plans to diversify the company, adding that the company did not "belittle" the loss of exclusivity "or the challenges that comes with it, related to the price pressure."

"We plan to come on the other side of the LOE as a bigger company than we are today and a much more diversified version of it," he said.

Stock Chart IconStock chart icon

Ahead of the opening bell on Monday, Novo shares had fallen 27% over the past 12 months, while its chief rival Eli Lilly shares have gained 52% over the same period.

Lilly has managed to grab a majority market share in the injectable GLP-1 space with Mounjaro and Zepbound, despite launching years after Novo's drugs.

While Novo's launched its Wegovy pill in the U.S. at the beginning of this year to great success, investors are still cautious around the drugmaker's prospects of regaining ground. It has begun to roll out the Wegovy pill in other markets as well, but it still represents a small portion of its total sales.

A series of clinical setbacks and leadership upheavals over the past year has added to investors' concerns.

watch now

Last week, Novo said it is rebranding from Novo Nordisk to Novo and updating its corporate culture. Doustdar told CNBC the rebrand and culture revamp were "parts of the same package" to meet fierce competition from Lilly.

Investors wanted more

Even as Novo indicates stable operating margins, Monday's announcement lacks the financial ambition the market wanted to see, Jacob Pedersen, investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, told CNBC.

"The investors, they are very particular in what they want from Novo, and this doesn't add up to it," Pedersen said, adding that Novo's target for growth in line with a broad group of pharma peers suggests slower growth than investors have historically come to expect from the company.

In August, Novo said it expects adjusted sales and operating profit to both be down 6% to flat in 2026, at constant exchange rates.

Analysts and investors have had mixed views on whether Novo should broaden its portfolio significantly, or focus on its existing therapy areas.

"It hasn't been long since the company wanted to focus more, and now they want to broaden out," Pedersen said.

The push to diversify marks a shift in the strategy Doustdar laid out after taking over as CEO last year, when Novo sharpened its focus on its core obesity and diabetes businesses and moved away from expanding into new areas.

Novo said Monday it is now moving beyond its core areas of obesity and diabetes. Doustdar said those remain Novo's foundation, but that the company now wants to build out its portfolio around blood and endocrine disorders, liver disease, and cardiovascular disease.

He also said Novo will be more active in business development, which was not included in the 2030 sales target.

- CNBC's Charlotte Reed and Mike Considine contributed to this report.

text:
EchoStar Corp.'s deals to sell airwave rights to AT&T and SpaceX highlight the political and regulatory pressures driving M&A activity, according to the lawyer who steered the transactions.

The company this year closed its transfer of about $40 billion worth of spectrum, resolving a Federal Communications Commission investigation into whether EchoStar slow-walked building its network. The deals came after President Donald Trump intervened in the probe, which EchoStar signaled could force it to file for bankruptcy.

“There was political intervention that resulted in the White House encouraging people to make a deal, and that’s what we did,” said Michael Deyong, a partner at White & Case who has advised EchoStar for nearly two decades. “We were able to get enough time to negotiate two deals at full value with AT&T and SpaceX, and they were just tremendous deals.”

The moves came during a tense stretch for EchoStar, which gained a stockpile of valuable spectrum when it acquired DISH Network in 2024. The company had spent billions of dollars and several years trying to build a nationwide communications network to compete with AT&T Inc. , Verizon Communications Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. EchoStar Chairman Charlie Ergen met directly with Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr to resolve the agency’s probe, Bloomberg News reported.

The spectrum deals are an example of the political and regulatory factors that are increasingly shaping M&A. Those pressures are weighing broadly across deals on which buyers to approach, what assets to sell, and how to structure transactions, said Deyong, the firm’s M&A co-head.

“We have to bring political and regulatory analysis forward into the transaction process,” Deyong said in an interview. “Instead of just treating governmental approvals as a post-signing condition, we have to assess the approval risk more so than ever, before even launching a sales process, before selecting bidders or before committing to a headline structure.”

M&A historically has been assessed through lenses such as commercial, financing, corporate, and antitrust, according to Deyong. Now, lawyers are getting calls ahead of bankers to help tackle issues related to ownership, governance, nationality, funding sources, security profiles, and regulator track records. They’re also being called on to assess whether sensitive assets, data, contracts or licenses need to be excluded from deals.

Lawyers are playing bigger roles in drafting communications around deals and are “helping to actually craft a narrative on everything” to account for any sensitivities around the structure, according to Deyong.

“The objective is not merely just to obtain approval, it’s to design a transaction that remains strategically sound,” he said.

‘Existential Threat’

Deyong, who is based in New York and was tapped to lead the firm’s M&A practice last year, considers himself a White & Case lifer. He started at the firm as a summer associate and has spent roughly 18 years there, excluding a stint at Linklaters.

For Deyong, the spectrum work shows off the expertise the firm has developed over a longterm relationship with EchoStar. He helped guide the company through its break up of two entities in 2008 and its reunion into a single entity 16 years later.

“I’ve been around long enough to split the companies into two public companies and then put the band back together,” Deyong said.

White & Case worked on nearly $103 billion in M&A transactions through the first half of the year, placing just inside the top 20 among Big Law’s deals advisers. Deyong focuses on representing public companies, including two that he has guided for most of his career: EchoStar and insurer Elevance Health Inc., formerly known as Anthem Inc.

The battle for spectrum has intensified as the demand for data balloons and large telecom companies like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile race to lock in long-term licenses. EchoStar’s deals with AT&T and SpaceX involve spectrum DISH gained when the Justice Department forced Sprint and T-Mobile to sell assets to clear their 2019 merger. The FCC’s investigation into whether EchoStar was meeting deadlines to build out its network raised the risk that the government could seek to reclaim the spectrum and sell it at auction.

“EchoStar really faced an existential threat,” Deyong said.

text:
Strategic collaboration accelerates Einride's push into highway and suburban autonomous trucking.

Einride will adapt the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion platform for heavy-duty trucking, working directly with NVIDIA to extend the platform's compute, sensor, software and safety architecture to the demands of heavy-duty freight.

Building the next generation of the Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion platform, will enable Einride to scale autonomous deployment across a freight network that's already serving customers today.

STOCKHOLM, Sept. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Einride AB (Nasdaq: ENRD) ("Einride" or the "Company"), a technology company driving the transition to cost-efficient autonomous and electric freight for some of the world's largest shippers, today announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to further accelerate the transition of the Company’s extensive freight network to autonomous operations.

Einride develops and integrates the technologies required to create cost-efficient autonomous and electric freight networks for its global shipping customers. Einride currently operates hundreds of electric trucks for major shippers across the U.S., Europe, and the Middle East, including autonomous trucks already operating in contracted customer deployments. This footprint is expected to scale to 1,500-2,000 vehicles by 2028, based on customer demand captured on its platform so far, and approximately 80% of that demand is suitable for automation in the medium term as the company continues to advance its autonomous technology.

Einride designs, builds, and operates the autonomous-driving system end-to-end, including safety validation, regulatory approval, and contracted customer deployments, while NVIDIA provides the underlying compute platform and AI development tools that support the system.

"We have the customers, the operational experience and the technology. Building the next generation of the Einride Driver on the NVIDIA Hyperion platform, will enable us to scale autonomous deployment across a freight network that's already serving customers today,“ said Henrik Green, Chief Technology Officer at Einride.

“Autonomous trucking represents one of the clearest opportunities to improve the safety and efficiency of global freight,” said Rishi Dhall, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. “By building on NVIDIA Hyperion with the NVIDIA Halos safety system and using NVIDIA Cosmos and Blackwell infrastructure, Einride can accelerate the development and validation of its autonomous-driving technology and scale deployments across its growing freight network.”

Built on the NVIDIA Hyperion platform, a production-ready compute and sensor reference architecture for Level 4 autonomy, and integrated with the NVIDIA Halos safety system, the collaboration creates a scalable foundation that accelerates safe, production-ready autonomous freight operations for Einride.

Einride intends to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell architecture at scale with an NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud partner, a cloud provider whose infrastructure NVIDIA has validated for large-scale AI training performance, to train, test and refine its autonomous driving models. This is a compute and development infrastructure that supports Einride’s own autonomous-driving stack.

Einride will adapt the NVIDIA Hyperion platform for heavy-duty trucking, working directly with NVIDIA to extend the platform's compute, sensor, software and safety architecture to the demands of heavy-duty freight. As part of its AI development workflow, Einride is using NVIDIA Cosmos to help improve the safety and reliability of its autonomous vehicles. NVIDIA Cosmos enables Einride to search and curate camera data to identify complex edge cases, as well as augment real-world data with photorealistic synthetic scenarios that increase the diversity of data used for AI training and validation.

About Einride

Founded in Stockholm in 2016, Einride (Nasdaq: ENRD) is a technology leader driving the transition to sustainable, cost-efficient autonomous and electric freight operations. The company’s platform integrates AI-powered freight intelligence, proprietary autonomous technology, and one of the world’s largest electric heavy-duty fleets. Einride serves a global customer base across North America, Europe, and the Middle East through a dual business model encompassing Freight-Capacity-as-a-Service (FCaaS) and a software platform.

text:
Novo Nordisk (NVO) shares are slimming down.

Shares of the Wegovy maker tanked more than 5% on Monday as the company failed to impress Wall Street at its capital markets day. The company came up short by not sharing more specifics around near-term growth targets amid fierce competition in the weight loss drug market.

The company said it's targeting more than $23 billion in pipeline sales by 2035. It has plans to launch more than five potential multi-blockbusters by the end of the decade.

"We have a situation where competition, as we are seeing it, has never been at least in Novo's historical back. For decades long, this company operated in what you could argue as a duopoly often. Thanks to us, we created an incredibly attractive market, and now almost every other single pharma company, big or small, is trying to come and compete with us. We need to be ready for that," Novo Nordisk CEO Mike Doustdar told investors.

Doustdar took over as CEO at Novo Nordisk in August 2025, succeeding longtime leader Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen. He has spent 33 years at Novo Nordisk, rising from an entry-level office clerk in Vienna in 1992 to the corner office.

In 2015, he was promoted to executive vice president of international operations, where he successfully managed the company's entire commercial business footprint outside the US and doubled sales across the division.

Today, Doustdar leads the global healthcare powerhouse as it navigates intense market competition in the GLP-1 market, mainly with rival Eli Lilly (LLY).

Doustdar said on the Power Players With Brian Sozzi podcast on Yahoo Finance earlier this month he is focused on improved marketing of Wegovy while continuing to build momentum behind its pill form, which fell short of analyst estimates in the most recent quarter.

He is also investing more aggressively in R&D to help overcome future patent expirations in the coming years.

Successfully pulling these things off will be paramount to getting Novo Nordisk's stock back in the good graces of investors who are worried about the company's future patent expiry cliff and how it will impact the bottom line.

"I would say, first I would like to see a future after the patent cliff where the majority of semaglutide sold is sold by Novo Nordisk. Today, Novo is the biggest generic insulin maker in the world," Doustdar said. "We don't have a monopoly of good ideas. So we're also looking into partnerships, acquisitions and trying to basically see where else we could compliment all the good things we have on our own."

text:
Three years into The New York Times’ copyright dispute with OpenAI and Microsoft, newly unredacted court filings have offered a closer look at how news material was gathered for AI training, and at concerns within the companies about the commercial consequences.

The documents, disclosed through a Times filing, describe large-scale collections of news articles, the use of material obtained through web indexes and allegations that researchers found ways to access paywalled content. They also contain internal assessments suggesting that generative AI could compete directly with publishers for audiences and revenue.

Much of the newly visible material comes from arguments made by The Times rather than the underlying exhibits, many of which remain sealed. The companies have not necessarily endorsed the characterisations made in the filing, and individual quotations can lack the surrounding context of the original documents.

Internal concerns over the publishers’ business

The potential impact on publishers is central to the legal dispute because US copyright law's fair-use doctrine considers, among other factors, whether an unauthorised use damages the market for the original work.

One Microsoft analysis cited by The Times examined traffic generated by its Copilot answer engine. According to the filing, click-through rates to The Times’ website fell by as much as 93 per cent compared with conventional Bing search. A January 2024 presentation by Microsoft applied the term “doom loop” to the problem, warning that reduced traffic could ultimately affect both publishers and the AI systems that depend on their material.

The presentation also acknowledged an unusual commercial dependency: Microsoft's AI business relies on a supply of externally produced information while potentially reducing the economic value of that same material.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella was also questioned in a deposition this year. According to the filing, he said paywalled material should be licensed when used for training or grounding. He further testified that, had he known OpenAI was training on paywalled material, he would have considered exercising Microsoft's contractual rights to require retraining.

OpenAI's own internal discussions, as presented by The Times, contain similarly stark assessments. Nick Turley, who leads ChatGPT, reportedly described the technology as posing an “existential threat” to publishers and said its products were becoming increasingly substitutive.

How the training material was assembled

The filings also provide figures illustrating the scale of material involved. The Times says OpenAI's mid-training datasets contained more than 91,692 copies of works published by the newspaper, The Daily News and the Center for Investigative Reporting. A separate dataset derived from Common Crawl allegedly contained more than two million documents originating from nytimes.com.

The material also describes collaboration between the two companies. According to the filing, OpenAI supplied its complete GPT-3 training dataset to Microsoft for evaluation and commercial development, while Microsoft supplied training data to OpenAI through projects known internally as Taxi and Mango.

The Times says data assembled through Project Mango included copies of at least 160,903 distinct works belonging to the publishers involved in the case.

Other datasets, including WebText and WebText2, allegedly contained substantial amounts of scraped news material. Common Crawl, an open web-crawling repository, was another source.

The filing further alleges that some training-data preparation involved removing copyright notices. Researchers were concerned, according to the material cited by The Times, about models reproducing those notices in their outputs.

Paywalls and the fair-use dispute

Perhaps the most contentious allegation concerns attempts to obtain material that was behind paywalls. The Times says an OpenAI researcher told Greg Brockman, the company's president, about a method for bypassing the New York Times paywall. Brockman's reported response was: “ah nice.”

The filing also cites a 2023 internal Microsoft memo by Brent Hecht, then a director of applied science, which characterised the scale of copying in exceptionally severe terms. Hecht described it as “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions” and referred to it as “the largest theft of labor in human history”.

Those statements are significant to the broader legal argument, but they do not by themselves determine whether the conduct breached copyright law.

Courts have been asked repeatedly to decide whether using copyrighted material to train AI models can qualify as fair use, with outcomes varying according to the facts and circumstances of individual cases. The legal question remains unsettled. The Times argues that the newly revealed evidence undermines key elements of OpenAI and Microsoft's defence, particularly where AI-generated answers substitute for visits to original publications.

Nadella acknowledged in testimony, according to the filing, that chatbot conversations can replace users going directly to the underlying website for information.

The case therefore reaches beyond the mechanics of training. It raises a broader question about whether systems built using journalism can ultimately weaken the economic model that funds that journalism. The latest disclosures add detail to that dispute, but the court's eventual treatment of the evidence will determine its legal significance.

text:
By Patrick Wingrove

LONDON, Sept 21 - Wegovy-maker Novo Nordisk's CEO Mike Doustdar will face pressure on Monday to set out his strategy for competing with US rival Eli Lilly and how he plans to boost the company's growth beyond the blockbuster weight-loss drug.

Novo rode ‌a wave of demand after launching Wegovy in 2021 which helped it become Europe's most valuable listed firm in 2023 with a market ‌capitalisation of more than $600 billion.

However, Novo's share price has plunged by more than 70% since its peak, while Lilly's has surged. Sales of the US drugmaker's rival Zepbound treatment are expected to outpace ​Wegovy this year by more than $7 billion, LSEG data shows.

Now, after trial setbacks and ahead of patent expiries in the early 2030s of semaglutide, the active ingredient in both Wegovy and its twin diabetes medicine Ozempic, investors want clarity on Novo's roadmap, including new growth areas.

"They should work harder in building a third leg ... because in diabetes and obesity, they won't find enough growth opportunities," said Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment, which has shares in both Novo and Lilly.

Novo should ‌diversify into therapeutic areas such as cardiovascular or rare diseases, ⁠Manns added.

Novo declined to comment.

'TOUGH TASK' TO CONVINCE INVESTORS

Doustdar, appointed just over a year ago, has moved to tighten costs, cull lagging or dead-end clinical programmes and seek targeted acquisitions and partnerships to rebuild a thinning late-stage pipeline.

While the launch of ⁠the Wegovy pill gave it momentum earlier this year, Novo suffered a major setback after halting trials of its experimental heart drug, ziltivekimab. This compounded concerns about Novo's long-term sales growth as the clock ticks down on patent protection, four analysts and investors said.

"It will be a very tough task actually to convince the market that the company ​is ​in really good shape because of the competition from Lilly, the price pressure, and also ​the patent expiry of semaglutide at the beginning of the ‌next decade," said Sydbank analyst Soren Lontoft Hansen.

BRUISING YEAR

Novo raised its sales and operating profit growth targets in August to between zero and minus 6% at constant exchange rates versus 2025, up from a previous range of minus 4% to minus 12%.

But its shares were sent tumbling in February on a trial setback for next-generation obesity drug CagriSema, its big hope to take over from Wegovy and help keep up with Lilly in the weight-loss market, which is estimated to be worth $100 billion or more by the early 2030s.

One investor said he wants Novo to break with recent practice and deliver concrete medium-term financial targets, pointing to ‌European rivals such as AstraZeneca, which has forecast $80 billion in annual group revenue by ​2030.

Analysts said they wanted a clearer roadmap to navigate rising competition from experimental obesity drugs developed ​by AstraZeneca and others, as well as the impending semaglutide patent cliff ​early next decade.

In the short term, Novo can lean on its Wegovy pill, which is holding onto a head start ‌over Lilly's Foundayo, although analysts warned the semaglutide-based treatment still gave ​only a temporary shield before patent expirations.

With ​Novo's late-stage pipeline sparse ahead of key trial readouts next year, analysts and investors said they expect management to signal a greater appetite for bolt-on acquisitions or licensing deals, warning that internal research and development alone cannot bridge the looming revenue gap.

Morningstar analyst Karen Andersen said Novo should ​focus more on promising early-pipeline candidate zenagamtide, rather than ‌continuing to pour money into CagriSema.

"They absolutely need to acquire something - I don't think they have enough power to do this all by ​their own. I'm not a big fan of tripling down in obesity ... they should buy something in other diseases," said Manns.

(Reporting by ​Patrick Wingrove in London; Editing by Josephine Mason, Adam Jourdan and Alexander Smith)

title: Jensen Huang: AI CEOs Have 'Ulterior Reasons' in Doomsday Warnings - Business Insider
description:
He accused the leaders of the frontier AI labs of being disingenuous in their warnings that, without more AI oversight, the products they are building could harm humanity in myriad forms.
"Go and read between the lines," Huang said, referring to AI leaders calling for government regulation of the industry.
Last week, a chorus of leading AI CEOs said AI development should be slowed down until adequate risk-prevention measures could be put in place.

text:
Don't let the black leather jacket fool you, Jensen Huang isn't a doomer.

Nvidia's CEO said as much in an interview with CBS News aired on Sunday. He accused the leaders of the frontier AI labs of being disingenuous in their warnings that, without more AI oversight, the products they are building could harm humanity in myriad forms.

"Go and read between the lines," Huang said, referring to AI leaders calling for government regulation of the industry. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have."

"They must be doing it for ulterior reasons," he added.

Huang said he didn't know exactly what those ulterior reasons are, but that scaring people about the tech is "irresponsible" and "unnecessary."

Huang's comments on Sunday echo those of President Donald Trump, who said on Saturday that new regulations aren't needed to ensure the tech remains safe.

"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," the president said on Truth Social, his social media platform.

Michael Kratsios, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, has also rejected the idea that tech companies need government intervention to ensure the safety of their AI models. In a Fox News interview on Sunday, he said the AI labs could just go ahead and "just stop" if they think their products are dangerous.

Last week, a chorus of leading AI CEOs said AI development should be slowed down until adequate risk-prevention measures could be put in place.

In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-pronged plan that would, in his view, strengthen safeguards to ensure AI remains under the control of human engineers.

One of those prongs included calls for the US government, "for antitrust reasons," to regulate frontier AI labs. Amodei's essay was signal-boosted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

Huang has emerged as a prominent anti-regulation voice, together with Trump and David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech.

In the CBS interview, Huang reiterated previous concerns that a slowdown among US labs would cede ground to China in the global AI race, and that AI labs don't need government help to implement a slowdown.

"We don't need more regulations," Huang said. "We need to apply the current regulations we have."
